# The relationship between technical support and teachers’ artiﬁcial intelligence self-e cacy: a psychological need mediation model grounded in self-determination theory

While existing research has predominantly examined the relationship between technical support and teachers’ AI self-e cacy, comparatively less attention **KEYWORDS** Artiﬁcial intelligence self- has been devoted to the association between teachers’ perceived satisfaction of eﬃcacy; technical support; psychological needs and their AI self-e cacy. Guided by Self-Determination Theory psychological needs (SDT), this study investigated the relationships among technical support, the satisfaction; self- satisfaction of psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and determination theory; K–12 teachers’ AI self-e cacy. Using structural equation modeling, we analyzed survey data teachers from 515 Chinese in-service K–12 teachers. Results indicated that while technical 

support did not show a signiﬁcant correlation with teachers’ AI self-e cacy, it was positively correlated with the satisfaction of three psychological needs. There is a 

statistically signiﬁcant positive association between the fulﬁllment of psychological needs and teachers’ AI self-e cacy. Moreover, the satisfaction of the three 

psychological needs mediates the relationship between technical support and AI self- e cacy. These ﬁndings provide empirical support for the applicability and explanatory 

power of SDT within the emerging context of AI education, and o er theoretical insights for future research on designing technology-supported environments.

# 1. Introduction

Against the backdrop of rapid technological advancements, artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a pivotal driver of innovation and transformation across various sectors (Choi & Kim, 2025). In the realm of edu- cation, AI presents novel opportunities for pedagogical reform and reshaping learning paradigms (Airaj, [2024)](#ethics-statement). However, there is currently a profound practical challenge: despite the global investment in AI edu- cational tools and the increasingly sophisticated technical support systems, frontline teachers’ actual depth of adoption, quality of integration, and sustained willingness to use AI technologies remain consistently below expectations. Empirical research has revealed that teachers’ AI self-e cacy is widely regarded as a critical antecedent to technology integration, yet its developmental trajectory exhibits high instability, often showing decline even after initial training interventions (Paetsch et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). This constitutes the core problem this study seeks to address: Why, despite extensive technical support interven- tions, does teachers’ AI self-e cacy remain di cult to stabilize, internalize, and sustain?

Existing research often simpliﬁes technical support into a direct external enabling tool, presupposing that it can linearly enhance teachers’ competence beliefs by providing knowledge, skills, and operational conven- ience (Bai et al., 2024; Hershkovitz et al., 2023). However, this “tool-to-e cacy” direct-path assumption proves inadequate in explaining the aforementioned practical paradox. Empirical evidence repeatedly demon- strates that mere technical provision often yields weak and transient e ects on teachers’ long-term self- e cacy (Peng et al., 2023).

To bridge this theoretical and practical gap, this study introduces Self-Determination Theory (SDT) as its core explanatory framework. SDT posits that high-quality motivation stems from the satisfaction of three

basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness (Choi et al., 2025). This theory o ers a crucial insight that transcends instrumental rationality: the e ectiveness of external support is not deter- mined by its objective attributes but by how it is subjectively perceived and experienced by individuals (Ma et al., 2025). When technical support is designed to nurture rather than undermine these three funda- mental needs, it can be truly internalized as autonomous motivation, thereby stably enhancing individuals’ AI self-e cacy.

Furthermore, against the backdrop of rapid global advancement in AI technologies, public attitudes toward AI exhibit pronounced cross-cultural variations – di erences that profoundly shape AI’s practical implementation in critical societal domains such as education. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artiﬁcial Intelligence’s (HAI) Artiﬁcial Intelligence Index Report reveals that Chinese citizens express signiﬁ- cantly higher levels of enthusiasm toward AI development than the global average, whereas English-speak- ing countries consistently report comparatively greater concern (Nestor et al. 2025). A parallel ﬁnding emerges from the global AI survey jointly conducted by the University of Melbourne and KPMG (Gillespie et al., 2025). Within the Chinese context, this enthusiasm for AI is deeply rooted in distinctive institutional arrangements and cultural values. China conceptualizes AI as a pivotal enabler of educational innovation, thereby cultivating fertile ground for its deep integration into education – and inevitably giving rise to socio- technical characteristics distinct from those observed in Western settings. Grounded in SDT, this study inves- tigates the relationships among AI self-e cacy, the satisfaction of three psychological needs, and perceived technical support among K–12 teachers in China.

# 2. Literature review and hypotheses

### _2.1 Self-determination theory and self-e_ _cacy_

Self-Determination Theory (SDT) serves as a classical theoretical framework for understanding intrinsic motivation and behavioral driving mechanisms, o ering crucial insights into the in uence of AI self- e cacy (Shi & Zhang, 2025; Yi & Siquan, 2025). According to its core principles (Ryan & Deci, 2000), human behavior is regulated by three fundamental psychological needs: autonomy (ownership and control over one’s actions and decisions), competence (successful completion of challenging tasks), and relatedness (the need for deep connections with others) (Ryan & Deci, 2000). In educational research, the satisfaction of these psychological needs is signiﬁcantly correlated with the development of learners’ artiﬁ- cial intelligence self-e cacy. For instance, when students received adequate autonomy, recognition of their abilities, and social support in educational practice, their willingness and conﬁdence in exploring and apply- ing AI technologies increased (Xia et al., 2023). Yi and Siquan (2025) found through structural equation mod- eling analysis of 562 preservice teachers that perceived autonomy, relatedness, and competence all positively predicted AI self-e cacy. Additionally, Xia et al. (2022) demonstrated that the SDT framework was valuable in enhancing learners’ AI preparation, boosting conﬁdence levels, fostering positive attitudes, alleviating technical anxiety, and reinforcing intrinsic motivation. However, current research primarily focuses on students and preservice teachers, with limited exploration of in-service teachers. Based on this gap, this study hypothesized that the experience of autonomy support, competence attainment, and relat- edness during AI technology application among in-service teachers may constitute pathways a ecting their AI self-e cacy. Consequently, this research proposed the following hypotheses. 

H1: A positive correlation exists between the satisfaction of the three psychological needs (autonomy, compe- tence, and relatedness) and teachers’ AI self-e cacy.

## _2.2 Technical support and self-determination theory_

The rapid advancement of AI technologies is profoundly reshaping the educational ecosystem, prompting growing scholarly attention to its impact on teachers’ professional psychology and instructional practices (Yi & Siquan, 2025). Empirical evidence indicates that many teachers experience signiﬁcant AI-related anxiety, which substantially undermines both their willingness and actual use of AI tools (Wu & Li, 2025). However, external support can mitigate such anxiety through sequential psychological mechanisms: by

Furthermore, institutional-level technical support serves as a critical enabler for satisfying teachers’ basic psychological need as posited by SDT (Wut et al., 2025). Prior research demonstrates that robust institutional support – including dedicated professional development time, non-punitive evaluation frameworks, and innovation-supportive organizational culture – enhances perceived relatedness and bu ers external pressure, thereby reinforcing autonomous motivation and competence beliefs (Viberg et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024). This institutional sca olding creates the necessary conditions for teachers to develop conﬁdence in their ability to integrate AI technologies e ectively into their teaching practices. Based on the synthesis of current literature and theoretical frameworks, this study proposes the following hypotheses. 

H2: A positive correlation exists between technical support and the satisfaction of the three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness).

### _2.3 Technical support and self-e_ _cacy_

In recent years, scholars have conducted in-depth discussions on the impact mechanism of AI technology in the ﬁeld of education, initially revealing the intrinsic relationship between technical support and tea- chers’ self-e cacy. Kim (2024), through qualitative research, found that when schools provided teachers with robust AI technical support, teachers could break through the limitations of traditional teaching models and exibly adjusted teaching strategies based on students’ heterogeneous learning needs, thus enhancing the innovation of classroom teaching. This ﬁnding aligned with the theoretical model pro- posed by Bailey et al. (2022), which suggested a signiﬁcant correlation between individuals’ technology acceptance, actual usage behavior, and their self-e cacy levels. Additionally, through a controlled trial and survey questionnaire involving over 300 students, Chiu et al. (2022) found that the satisfaction of three needs (autonomy, relatedness, and competence) played mediation between technical support and digital literacy. Although that study focused on student groups, it could be inferred that for teacher groups, the satisfaction of three needs played mediation between technical support and AI self-e cacy. All the above research ﬁndings indicate that sound technical support can enable teachers to develop a positive perception of new technologies, thereby enhancing their AI self-e cacy and encouraging them to actively apply AI technologies in teaching practice. Based on these ﬁndings, this study proposes the following hypotheses. 

H3: A positive correlation exists between technical support and teachers’ AI self-e cacy.

H4: The satisfaction of the needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) mediates the relationship between technical support and teachers’ AI self-e cacy.

# 3. Method

## _3.1 Participants_

This study employed snowball sampling, a non-probability sampling technique particularly well-suited for accessing hard-to-reach or hidden populations (Gierczyk et al., 2024). All participants were required to meet two a priori inclusion criteria: (1) current employment as a K–12 teacher, and (2) engagement with at least one form of AI-related professional development or AI-integrated instructional tool within the past 12 months. The ﬁnal analytic sample comprised _N_ = 515 valid responses, geographically distributed across 31 provinces in China. Survey invitations were disseminated via an online questionnaire platform; initial “seed” participants shared the survey link within their professional networks. To ensure data quality and mitigate the inherent risks of self-selection bias and inattentive responding common in online surveys, a two-stage validation protocol was implemented. The ﬁrst stage involved prescreening items designed to verify occupational status (i.e. active K–12 teacher). The second stage incorporated embedded attention-check items to identify and subsequently exclude random or inattentive responders. [Table 1](#3-method) pre- sents detailed demographic information regarding the sample.

## _3.2 Instrument_

The questionnaire was structured into four distinct sections, each serving a speciﬁc purpose in the research. The ﬁrst section gathered demographical information from the participants. This included details such as gender, teaching seniority, academic qualiﬁcations, education phase, school type, weekly AI usage duration, and total accumulated AI usage time. The second section assessed teachers’ perceived technical support in the context of AI education. The third section comprised questions designed to measure teachers’ AI self-e cacy. The fourth section assessed three psychological needs as speciﬁed by self-determination theory: perceived autonomy, perceived competence, and perceived relatedness. To measure the responses in the questionnaire, a 5-point Likert scale was employed. This scale was based on the criteria proposed by Brown (2010), ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”.

### _3.2.1 Technical support_

In the ﬁeld of AI education research, technical support emerges as an important factor. It refers to the pro- vision of assistance for any technical issues that teachers may encounter during their teaching processes. This study employed a subscale from Lee et al.’s (2011) perceived support scale to measure teachers’ percep- tions of technical support. The construct primarily assesses teachers’ perceived availability of timely and sup- portive resources that fulﬁll their psychological needs. Speciﬁcally, it encompasses school technical troubleshooting capacity and teachers’ perceived ease of use of AI tools. This conceptualization is grounded in the theoretical framework of SDT.

While this instrument was originally designed for student populations, it demonstrates adaptability in the novel context of AI education where teachers themselves function as technology learners facing analogous challenges. From a theoretical perspective, Self-Determination Theory (SDT) explicitly posits that autonomy, competence, and relatedness constitute three innate and universal basic psychological needs whose satis- faction is fundamental to fostering intrinsic motivation, well-being, and psychological health. This robust theoretical framework has demonstrated extensive applicability far beyond the student population, with empirical validation across diverse contexts including the workplace, healthcare settings, sports, and family relationships (Laguerre & Barnes-Farrell, 2025; Schrooyen et al., 2024; Wannheden et al., 2021). Con- sequently, the adaptation of validated scales measuring these three core needs from student populations to teacher populations is theoretically sound.

Moreover, this study conducted strict reliability and validity tests on the measurement results, the results showed that the reliability and validity met relevant standards. Consequently, we contend that these adapted items e ectively capture teachers’ perceived access to technical support within AI educational environments.

### _3.2.2 Needs satisfaction_

The needs satisfaction scale employed in this study was adapted from the instrument developed by Hew and Kadir (2016). This scale comprises three primary dimensions: perceived autonomy, perceived competence, and perceived relatedness. An illustrative item for perceived autonomy is “My feelings toward AI are taken into consideration at work”. For perceived competence, an example item reads “Most days I feel a sense of accomplishment from working with AI”. Lastly, a representative item for perceived relatedness states “People at work care about me”.

#### _3.2.3 Artiﬁcial intelligence self-e_ _cacy_

The artiﬁcial intelligence self-e cacy scale covers four distinct measuring aspects: assistance, anthropo- morphic interaction, comfort with AI, and technological skills. These dimensions have been developed from Wang and Chuang (2024). Regarding the assistance dimension, an example item is “I’m conﬁdent in my ability to learn simple programming of AI technologies/products if I were provided the necessary train- ing”. For the anthropomorphic interaction aspect, an illustrative item is “I think the way that AI technologies/ products express content when interacting is unique, just like a real person”. This item measures teachers’ contextualized e cacy beliefs regarding the perceived reliability of AI interactions – a construct distinct from general attitudes toward AI. Shamsuddinova et al. (2024) provided corroborating evidence that when teachers perceive AI as capable of understanding pedagogical needs “like a real person”, such percep- tion signiﬁcantly enhances their willingness to integrate AI tools and strengthens their e cacy expectations. In terms of comfort with AI, an example could be “When interacting with AI technologies/products, I feel comfortable in my heart”. For the technological skills dimension, an instance could be expressed as “When using an AI technology/product, there is nothing that I do not know why”.

The integration of the four sub-dimensions into a single latent variable is grounded in three consider- ations. From a theoretical perspective, the four sub-dimensions of AI self-e cacy are not independent con- structs but rather an integrated system. For individuals, their perceived self-e cacy in using artiﬁcial intelligence is a comprehensive perception that transcends these subdimensions. This viewpoint is sup- ported by existing research, which suggests that users’ self-e cacy is more likely to manifest as a dominant general factor (Wang & Chuang, 2024). In terms of empirical evidence, the original scale development research has veriﬁed that the four sub-dimensions jointly represent self-e cacy (Wang & Chuang, 2024). 

6 L. XIE AND H. ZHANG

The data analysis of this study indicated that the single-dimensional model reached an acceptable ﬁtting level, and indicators such as CFI and RMSEA reached the recognized threshold range. In terms of the research objective, the original intention of this study is to examine the mediating mechanism of SDT in explaining the emerging educational phenomenon of teachers’ adoption of AI technology. The use of a single factor helps to clearly present the main path of action. Future research will employ longitudinal or multi-group designs to investigate potential di erential e ects of SDT on each sub-dimension.

## _3.3 Data analysis_

This study utilized two software programs, Mplus 8.3 and SPSS 25, for data analysis. At the outset, SPSS 25 was used for descriptive statistics, correlations analysis, and Cronbach’s alpha coe cients analysis. These analyses not only provided a fundamental understanding of the data characteristic but also served as a means to verify the reliability of the questionnaire employed in this study. Following this initial phase, Mplus 8.3 was used for conﬁrmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling. Additionally, bootstrapping was employed to test mediation e ects. All these analytical procedures were of paramount importance when it came to rigorously testing both the reliability and validity of the measurement models established in this study, along with comprehensively evaluating the intricate structural relationships existing between various variables under investigation.

# 4. Results

## _4.1 Descriptive statistics and reliability and validity testing_

The mean value, standard deviation, and correlation of the measurement results were shown in [Table 2.](#33-data-analysis) The vales of skewness ranged from −0.07 to 0.09. The values of kurtosis ranged from −0.22 to 0.06. Furthermore, the _p_-value of each correlation coe cient was lower than 0.01, indicating a statistically signiﬁcant positive relationship between the variables under investigation.

The constructs in the proposed model were subjected to rigorous assessments of reliability and validity. As indicated in [Table 3,](#42-common-method-bias-testing) all CRs exceeded 0.80, all AVEs exceeded 0.60, and all Cronbach’s alpha coe cients exceeded 0.90. The ﬁndings collectively demonstrated that all constructs satisﬁed the requirements set forth by Fornell and Larcker (1981), thereby a rming their internal consistency and convergent validity at a high level. To assess the convergent validity of the dimensions in the measuring model, conﬁrmatory factor analy- sis (CFA) was performed. The results demonstrated an excellent ﬁt for the model, with the following indices: CFI = 0.992, TLI = 0.992, RMSEA = 0.021, and SRMR = 0.024. Such statistics provided compelling evidence that the proposed measuring model demonstrated satisfactory levels of reliability and validity.

In addition to assessing reliability and validity, discriminant validity was also examined. The outcomes of this analysis are presented in [Table 4.](#42-common-method-bias-testing) Speciﬁcally, it was found that the square root of the AVE was greater than the correlation between each construct and other components in the model. This indicates that the constructs possess adequate discriminant validity. Overall, based on these comprehensive analyses, the pro- posed measuring model demonstrated robust levels of both reliability and validity.

## _4.2 Common method bias testing_

This study employed a dual-validation strategy to assess common method bias, thereby ensuring the robust- ness of the ﬁndings. First, we conducted a single-factor conﬁrmatory factor analysis. The results yielded RMSEA = 0.117 (\>0.08), CFI = 0.749 (\<0.95), TLI = 0.735 (\<0.95), and SRMR = 0.104 (\>0.08), collectively indicat- ing that the present study is not susceptible to common method bias. Second, we further implemented a bifactor conﬁrmatory factor analysis model. Building upon the original CFA model, we incorporated a method factor such that all observed indicators loaded simultaneously onto both their respective trait factors and the common method factor. The results indicated that the model ﬁt indices after incorporating the method factor were RMSEA = 0.021, CFI = 0.992, TLI = 0.992, and SRMR = 0.028. These values were com- parable to those of the baseline model without the method factor (RMSEA = 0.021, CFI = 0.992, TLI = 0.992, and SRMR = 0.019), with no statistically or substantively meaningful improvement in model ﬁt. This ﬁnding suggests that common method bias is negligible in the present dataset.

### _4.3 Mediating e_ _ect analysis_

This study employed maximum likelihood (ML) estimation, a method widely recognized for its robustness in structural equation modeling under conditions of multivariate normality and adequate sample size. The hypothesized mediation model was grounded in SDT, ensuring strong theoretical grounding by including only core constructs and their a-priori hypothesized relationships, thereby avoiding data-driven overparame- terization. The SEM results indicated that the model depicted in [Figure 1](#23-technical-support-and-self-e-cacy) provided a good ﬁt for the data (_χ_[^2]/ df = 1.224, CFI = 0.992, TLI = 0.992, SRMR = 0.024, and RMSEA = 0.021) (Maydeu-Olivares, 2017). These indices collectively indicate that the theoretically constrained model adequately reproduces the observed covari- ance structure without su ering from underﬁt due to oversimpliﬁcation. [Figure 2](#5-discussion) and [Table 5](#5-discussion) present the model path coe cients, standardized direct, indirect and total e ects identiﬁed among the variables.

The analysis revealed signiﬁcant positive correlation of technical support and three psychological needs. Specially, technical support was signiﬁcantly correlated with perceived autonomy (_β_ = 0.550, _p_ \< 0.001), per- ceived competence (_β_ = 0.552, _p_ \< 0.001), and perceived relatedness (_β_ = 0.415, _p_ \< 0.001). These ﬁndings provide strong support for the hypothesis H2. In contrast, there was no signiﬁcant relationship between technical support and teachers’ AI self-e cacy (_β_ = −0.065, _p_ = 0.229). Consequently, the hypothesis H3 was rejected. Furthermore, each three psychological needs – autonomy (_β_ = 0.393, _p_ \< 0.001), competence (_β_ = 0.359, _p_ \< 0.001), and relatedness (_β_ = 0.294, _p_ \< 0.001) – was correlated with teachers’ AI self-e cacy. Thus the hypothesis H1 was conﬁrmed.

**Figure 2.** Model path coeﬃcients.

To determine the mediating role of psychological needs satisfaction, we used a bootstrapping approach with 2000 random samples and calculated 95% conﬁdence intervals (CI) for the indirect e ects. The total e ect of technical support on AI self-e cacy was 0.472 (_p_ \< 0.001). The indirect e ects of technical support mediated through perceived autonomy (_β_ = 0.216, _p_ \< 0.001), perceived competence (_β_ = 0.198, _p_ \< 0.001), and perceived relatedness (_β_ = 0.122, _p_ \< 0.001) were all signiﬁcant, whereas the direct e ect of technical support on AI self-e cacy was not signiﬁcant (_β_ = −0.065, _p_ \> 0.05). The 95% Cis for the indirect e ects did not include zero, conﬁrming that the satisfaction of psychological needs signiﬁcantly mediated the relationship between technical support and AI self-e cacy (H4).

The direct association between technological support and AI self-e cacy shifted from a positive corre- lation (_r_ = 0.44) to near-zero in the full model – a pattern inconsistent with classical suppression. Crucially, psychological needs are theoretically well-grounded as a mediator. According to SDT, technical support that satisfy teachers’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness foster stronger e cacy beliefs toward emerging technologies. In our model, the association between technological support and AI self- e cacy vanished upon inclusion of psychological needs – indicating that psychological needs constitute the core psychological mechanism through which technological support translates into e cacy beliefs, rather than functioning as a suppressor. Furthermore, the maximum variance in ation factor (VIF) among all endogenous variables was 1.731, ruling out multicollinearity as a source of estimation bias. Finally, overall model ﬁt indices were excellent, providing robust support for the theoretical speciﬁcation.

# 5. Discussion

This study, grounded in SDT, investigates the intricate mechanisms linking technical support, the satisfaction of psychological needs, and teachers’ AI self-e cacy. The ﬁndings reveal a critical mediating pathway: tech- nical support signiﬁcantly enhances teachers’ satisfaction of the three psychological needs – autonomy,

competence, and relatedness – within AI educational contexts, which in turn indirectly strengthens their AI self-e cacy. This result provides robust empirical validation for the applicability of SDT in the emerging domain of AI education.

This study conﬁrms a signiﬁcant positive association between technical support and the satisfaction of the three psychological needs. This ﬁnding robustly corroborates a core tenet of SDT – namely, that a supportive environment is a critical precondition for fulﬁlling individuals’ intrinsic psychological needs and fostering high-quality motivation (Ahn et al., [2021)](#ethics-statement). This result aligns with prior empirical evidence in the ﬁeld (Xia et al., 2022). Within the context of AI education, when teachers perceive that the AI tools provided by their schools are user-friendly, adequately resourced, and accompanied by timely and e ective support channels, they are more likely to experience a sense of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in their instructional practice.

The ﬁndings reveal signiﬁcant positive associations between the fulﬁllment of the three psychological needs and AI self-e cacy. This result aligns with prior empirical evidence (Chiu, 2024; Du & Alm, 2024). When individuals perceive that a technological tool satisﬁes their needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, they are more likely to develop robust self-e cacy beliefs regarding AI use.

This study ﬁnds that the satisfaction of the three psychological needs mediates the relationship between technical support and AI self-e cacy. Notably, no statistically signiﬁcant direct association was observed between technical support and AI self-e cacy. This ﬁnding stands in contrast to an implicit assumption com- monly embedded in studies grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) – namely, that enhanced technical support directly translates into greater behavioral intention or heightened self-e cacy (Aldrai- weesh & Alturki, [2025)](#ethics-statement). We posit that this result illuminates a critical pain point in China’s current AI edu- cation landscape: a profound misalignment between the supply of technical resources and teachers’ authentic pedagogical needs.

From a policy perspective, the State Council of China and the Ministry of Education have issued multiple strategic directives on AI education, establishing a robust institutional framework that facilitates teachers’ access to and adoption of AI technologies. This top-down policy implementation model has demonstrably succeeded in infrastructure development and resource dissemination. However, it frequently operates under a “supply-driven” rather than a “demand-driven” logic (Liu & Shang, 2025). Consequently, such initiatives often overlook teachers’ core concerns regarding the adaptability of AI tools to speciﬁc classroom contexts and their seamless integration into instructional practice (Xie & Luo, 2025).

Culturally, the Chinese educational context places emphasis on the teacher’s authoritative role. When AI tools are designed as substitutes for teachers – as opposed to augmentative or supportive partners – they risk triggering professional identity anxiety and resistance toward technology adoption (Ho & Lee, 2025). The absence of a direct e ect observed in this study does not imply that technological support is unimportant; rather, it reveals a more nuanced proposition. In the Chinese context, e ective technological support must transcend mere provision of tools and evolve into a responsive support paradigm – one that precisely addresses teachers’ psychological needs and professional concerns within authentic teaching scenarios.

# 6. Conclusion and limitation

This study investigates how Chinese K–12 teachers’ perceptions of psychological need satisfaction, as con- ceptualized within SDT, mediate the relationship between technical support and their AI self-e cacy. The ﬁndings reveal a statistically signiﬁcant positive association between the fulﬁllment of SDT psychological needs and teachers’ AI self-e cacy. Furthermore, technical support demonstrates a signiﬁcant positive cor- relation with the satisfaction of these psychological needs. Critically, the satisfaction of SDT psychological needs fully mediates the relationship between technical support and AI self-e cacy, underscoring its pivotal role in facilitating teachers’ e ective integration of AI into instructional practice. This mediation e ect provides compelling empirical evidence for the applicability of SDT in the emerging context of AI- enhanced education. In advancing the implementation of AI education within K–12 settings, policymakers and school administrators should move beyond a narrow focus on mere technological provision and instead prioritize the deliberate cultivation of a supportive environment that actively fulﬁlls teachers’ psycho- logical needs.

10 L. XIE AND H. ZHANG

This study has four limitations. First, while this study primarily focused on basic psychological needs within SDT, it did not account for other potential in uencing factors such as motivational behaviors (Ahmadi et al., [2023)](#ethics-statement), discipline, policy (Ravšelj et al., 2025) etc. Future research should broaden existing theoretical frameworks to incorporate more variables. Second, the sample in this study was recruited via snowball sampling and may be skewed toward a subgroup of teachers who are more open to educational technology. Consequently, caution is warranted when generalizing these ﬁndings to contexts characterized by strong technological resistance or severe resource constraints. Third, although the AI self-e cacy scale employed in this study has been empirically validated, certain items may predominantly capture dimensions of perception and attitude rather than beliefs about one’s capabilities. Future research will reﬁne this scale to disentangle the constructs of perception and belief. Fourth, the sample for this study was drawn from China, where AI education is characterized by a uniﬁed curriculum framework, policy guidance, and collaborative lesson planning practices – factors that collectively shape teachers’ perceptions of and behaviors toward AI technologies. Consequently, the ﬁndings may not be generalizable to educational systems lacking standar- dized curricula and institutional support for AI integration.

# Ethics statement

The studies involving humans were approved by Shenzhen Polytechnic University. The studies were con- ducted in accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. The cover page of the ques- tionnaire explicitly outlined the study’s purpose, the voluntary nature of participation, conﬁdentiality protocols, and the right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Completion of the questionnaire was taken as implicit consent to participate in the research.

No potential con ict of interest was reported by the author(s).
